title: Physicians treated Joseph Coates’s POEMS syndrome with three drugs that an early Every Cure algorithm also ranked highly, allowing a later stem cell transplant and remission
summary: Mr. Joseph Coates received three drugs (i) that a consulting physician had considered and (ii) that Every Cure’s early drug-repurposing system had scored highly.
account: In January 2024, Joseph Coates, 37, of Renton, Washington, was critically ill with POEMS syndrome. His heart and kidneys were failing, and he was too sick for a stem cell transplant. His partner, Tara Theobald, asked David Fajgenbaum of the University of Pennsylvania and Every Cure for help. Fajgenbaum considered three drugs used for multiple myeloma, a related disease. He later explained that an early Every Cure algorithm also scored those drugs highly for POEMS. He recommended carfilzomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone to Coates’s treating hematologist and oncologist, Wayne Gao, who agreed to administer them. Coates later reported that he responded within one or two weeks and left intensive care three weeks later. He recovered enough to receive a stem cell transplant and reported full remission five months after that transplant. The New York Times reported improvement within a week and transplant eligibility about four months later. A brief vignette in The Lancet Haematology describes a matching unnamed patient and labels the result unpublished data. The sources support a contribution from AI alongside the physicians’ judgment, but they do not establish the exact model release or isolate its effect on recovery.
purpose: Every Cure uses AI to rank existing drugs as candidates for other diseases. Its early algorithms helped Fajgenbaum assess drugs that he had considered for Coates’s POEMS syndrome. The New Yorker notes that Every Cure does not usually make recommendations for individual patients.
developer: Every Cure (co-founded by David Fajgenbaum, University of Pennsylvania)
deployer: David Fajgenbaum (Every Cure / University of Pennsylvania); regimen administered by Wayne Gao, Coates's treating hematologist and oncologist
segment: Individual off-label treatment of a terminal POEMS syndrome patient

ratings.reason: Coates was critically ill, too sick for a transplant, and facing hospice care. He reported that he began responding to the drug regimen within one or two weeks, later received a stem cell transplant, and reached full remission five months after that transplant. The reported benefit was life-preserving. The available evidence does not isolate AI’s contribution from clinical judgment, the drugs, supportive care, or the transplant.

ai_role.statement: Fajgenbaum said that he had considered three drugs used for multiple myeloma and that Every Cure’s AI algorithm also scored them highly for POEMS syndrome. In an earlier AAMC interview, he described reviewing the scores and recommending the drugs to Coates’s treating physician. Wayne Gao weighed the risks and administered the treatment. The AI therefore supported the physicians’ assessment of candidate drugs. The sources do not show that it independently devised the regimen or that the benefit would have been impossible without it. The Lancet Haematology commentary contains a brief vignette of a matching unnamed POEMS patient, explicitly labeled unpublished data. No detailed clinical case report, underlying medical records, or case-specific model output was located. The commentary names KGML-xDTD as one of several algorithms in Every Cure’s platform, but it does not establish which algorithm or release was used for Coates.

limitations: No detailed clinical case report, underlying medical records, drug doses, or case-specific model output for Coates was located. The Lancet commentary contains a brief unnamed vignette and explicitly labels the result unpublished data.

The sources do not isolate AI’s contribution from the physicians’ judgment, the drug regimen, supportive care, and later transplantation. Coates places full remission five months after his transplant.

MATRIX names the platform, but the precise algorithm and release used in January 2024 remain unknown. KGML-xDTD is one of several algorithms described later, not an established identification of the model used for Coates.

The unnamed patients in WHYY, the Lancet commentary, and ARPA-H are matched to Coates by context. These identifications remain inferences. ARPA-H’s relative date differs from the January 2024 chronology.

The NYT and Every Cure annual report say that improvement began within a week and that transplant eligibility followed about four months later. Coates recalls a response within one or two weeks in the documentary. The Lancet vignette gives nine months of remission at submission without a submission date or definition that reconciles it with Coates’s post-transplant timeline.
The medical commentary, institutional film, and additional interviews share investigators or witnesses. Their publication in different outlets does not establish independent clinical confirmation.

claim_chains.finding: The NYT article, its archived English copy, and the licensed Infobae translation are one reporting origin. The original includes testimony from Coates and Wayne Gao. The New Yorker has its own interview. Penn Medicine adds original patient and partner testimony and earlier patient videos. AAMC and WHYY add earlier interviews with Fajgenbaum. The Lancet commentary gives a brief vignette labeled unpublished data. These sources are original accounts, but their shared witnesses and institutional relationships do not constitute independent clinical replication.

Fajgenbaum says in the documentary that he had considered the drugs and that AI also scored them highly. His September 2024 AAMC interview describes reviewing the scores before recommending drugs and explicitly dates Joseph’s crisis to January. WHYY’s March 2024 account describes a matching unnamed Washington patient about six weeks after the appeal. These accounts support AI-assisted assessment alongside clinical judgment, not the claim that AI alone invented an untested regimen.

Every Cure identifies an early version of its algorithms for the January 2024 treatment. A January 30 interview describes multiple algorithms, including Elsevier contributions, without identifying which produced Coates’s scores. WHYY names MATRIX in March 2024. Neither that platform name nor the later KGML-xDTD documentation establishes the algorithm or release used for Coates.

claim_chains.claim: Treatment novelty and the separate summer-2024 conference report
claim_chains.finding: A 2021 JACC case report describes the same three drugs for a different POEMS patient. EHA abstract PB2758 reports a separate eight-patient Qilu Hospital cohort, with seven responses. Neither source reports AI involvement. The EHA abstract is a plausible match for Every Cure’s uncited conference reference, but that match remains an inference. Both are clinical context, not evidence about Coates or independent verification of his AI-assisted recommendation.

limitations: No detailed clinical case report, underlying medical records, drug doses, or case-specific model output for Coates was located. The Lancet commentary contains a brief unnamed vignette and explicitly labels the result unpublished data.

The sources do not isolate AI’s contribution from the physicians’ judgment, the drug regimen, supportive care, and later transplantation. Coates places full remission five months after his transplant.

MATRIX names the platform, but the precise algorithm and release used in January 2024 remain unknown. KGML-xDTD is one of several algorithms described later, not an established identification of the model used for Coates.

The unnamed patients in WHYY, the Lancet commentary, and ARPA-H are matched to Coates by context. These identifications remain inferences. ARPA-H’s relative date differs from the January 2024 chronology.

The NYT and Every Cure annual report say that improvement began within a week and that transplant eligibility followed about four months later. Coates recalls a response within one or two weeks in the documentary. The Lancet vignette gives nine months of remission at submission without a submission date or definition that reconciles it with Coates’s post-transplant timeline.
The medical commentary, institutional film, and additional interviews share investigators or witnesses. Their publication in different outlets does not establish independent clinical confirmation.

fields.summary: Mr. Joseph Coates received three drugs (i) that a consulting physician had considered and (ii) that Every Cure’s early drug-repurposing system had scored highly.
fields.account: In January 2024, Joseph Coates, 37, of Renton, Washington, was critically ill with POEMS syndrome. His heart and kidneys were failing, and he was too sick for a stem cell transplant. His partner, Tara Theobald, asked David Fajgenbaum of the University of Pennsylvania and Every Cure for help. Fajgenbaum considered three drugs used for multiple myeloma, a related disease. He later explained that an early Every Cure algorithm also scored those drugs highly for POEMS. He recommended carfilzomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone to Coates’s treating hematologist and oncologist, Wayne Gao, who agreed to administer them. Coates later reported that he responded within one or two weeks and left intensive care three weeks later. He recovered enough to receive a stem cell transplant and reported full remission five months after that transplant. The New York Times reported improvement within a week and transplant eligibility about four months later. A brief vignette in The Lancet Haematology describes a matching unnamed patient and labels the result unpublished data. The sources support a contribution from AI alongside the physicians’ judgment, but they do not establish the exact model release or isolate its effect on recovery.
